claim: In a 400+ developer enterprise deployment of GitHub Copilot, the average acceptance rate was 33% for suggestions and 20% for lines of code, with 72% developer satisfaction.
stance_target: establishes the real-world magnitude of baseline acceptance-rate metrics against which any confidence-communication intervention's uplift should be measured
scope_conditions: Zoominfo enterprise engineering organization, 400+ developers, multiple programming languages, four-phase deployment
quoted_support: The results show an average acceptance rate of 33% for suggestions and 20% for lines of code, with high developer satisfaction scores of 72%.

claim: This real-world enterprise Copilot deployment study reports no confidence, uncertainty, or calibration signal being surfaced to developers at all -- acceptance decisions are made purely on the developer's own read of the raw code suggestion.
stance_target: gap: current large-scale industrial AI coding tools do not expose any calibrated confidence signal to end users, an open opportunity the target paper's prescriptive interface could address
scope_conditions: Zoominfo Copilot deployment; inferred from absence of any calibration/confidence mention in the abstract
quoted_support: Our analysis combines both quantitative metrics, focusing on acceptance rates of suggestions given by GitHub Copilot and qualitative feedback given by developers through developer satisfaction surveys.

claim: Acceptance-rate performance varies by programming language and deployment context in real enterprise settings, implying any confidence-communication intervention's payoff should be measured across languages, not on a single benchmark language.
stance_target: methodological caveat for generalizability of any single-language evaluation of a prescriptive confidence method
quoted_support: We also discuss language-specific performance variations, limitations, and lessons learned from this medium-scale enterprise deployment.
